The nest picker does not lead him through the wedge, it names it. mvm_mannworks.cfg EngineerNest 4 is "1014 885 256", the wedge coordinate one step lower, and 1014 885 has no nav area over it. It is an unmeshed pocket walled by ground 11 to 25 units away on every side.

A path there ends at the edge of the hole, so the arrival test never comes true, every re-pick sends him back, and that is the DefenderBuildSentrygun under DefenderEngineerIdle loop the crash dumps land in.

The fix is a config edit, not a behaviour change. Verified: the coordinate is exactly that in the file.
CAUSE FOUND offline, mvm-z83.27. mvm_mannworks.cfg EngineerNest 4 is "1014 885 256" and 1014 885 has no nav area over it: an unmeshed pocket walled by ground 11 to 25 units away on every side. A path there ends at the edge of the hole, the arrival test never comes true, every re-pick sends him back, and that is the DefenderBuildSentrygun under DefenderEngineerIdle loop in the crash dumps. The picker does not lead him through the wedge, it names it. Config edit, not a behaviour change. Coordinate verified against the file.

title: Nothing records what killed a defender, or how far an upgrade got
description:
mvm-gwq closed on a measurement that also showed what the test-bed cannot see.
Two questions came out of it and neither can be answered today:

- **A resistance is bought, but to what tier?** One tier may not be enough
  against the wave that killed the bot. Nothing logs the level each bot reaches
  on each upgrade, so "they buy it" and "they buy enough of it" are the same
  line in the results.
- **What killed the defender?** testbed/results/ records deaths per wave and
  not their cause. A Scout dying to something a resistance does not cover looks
  exactly like a Scout dying because the resistance was too cheap to buy.

Both are one field each in the wave result. Until they exist, any bead of the
form "the bots do not buy enough X" is unfalsifiable, which is how mvm-gwq sat
at P0 on a premise that turned out to be wrong.

Third thing worth a look while in there: nine of the 38 trips ended with "the
game refused one". The upgrade file says a refusal repeats until the window
closes, so a bot that hits one may be spending less than it could.

title: The pyro dies in five seconds at close range
description:
Discord, 2026-08-27.

k-kaneta: "I'm finding out that Pyro is glorified medium ammo box outside of
tank wave in the hard way", "they w+m1 and die in 5 seconds like human
counterpart"

omaewh4: "yeah their close range AI is simple"

## What it means

The pyro walks in holding fire and dies. No airblast, no retreat, no reading of
what it is walking into. It is worth a seat on a tank wave and close to nothing
otherwise, so a lineup with one is playing five against the wave.

mvm-abf already covers the pyro's upgrade priorities. This is the behaviour
rather than what it buys.

title: Bots fall off Rottenburg
description:
Discord, 2026-08-27, k-kaneta on Rottenburg: "I nearly fell and I believe one of
the ai actually fell lol", with a screenshot of the bridge.

A bot that falls is a seat lost for a respawn and whatever it was carrying. The
map is Valve's, so the nav is the game's own and the fall is the mod walking a
route the nav allows and a body cannot survive.

title: Play-test the Bot Switcher with somebody on RED
description:
mvm-6dc is built and measured, but every measurement was taken on the test-bed
with nobody playing. One thing that cannot be measured that way:

A human takes seat one, and the switcher renumbers seats around whoever is
there. The seat a player holds is the seat the composition counts from, so a
lineup typed while somebody is on RED is the case with the most room to be
wrong and the least coverage.

What to check on a real server:

- swap a seat while a human is on RED and confirm the human keeps his place
- swap mid-wave and confirm it waits for the break rather than dropping
  buildings
- confirm the replacements come back with the money they had earned, which was
  measured with bots only
- !ap bots from a client, not rcon, since the menu path differs

Closing mvm-6dc on the build and leaving this open is the same shape as mvm-8ws
and mvm-15t: the work ships, the confirmation is its own bead.

title: The test-bed calls an install-time restart a crash
description:
run.sh ends with "the game server has crashed N time(s): that is a bug in what
is being measured, not a slow wave", and it gets N by counting "core dumped"
lines in the container log.

Most of those are not crashes in anything being measured. The test-bed installs
the mod and the statistics plugin and the server restarts around it, and every
one of those restarts leaves a "core dumped" line behind. They are all preceded
by "installed the bots and the statistics plugin".

It cost an evening. A reseat feature looked like it was crashing the server
across three runs, and the count was the only evidence. The one crash that
actually happened during play was the engine watchdog:

  [defenderbots] stuck: Waldo (engineer) ... for 12s, DefenderEngineerIdle
  WatchDog! Server took too long to process (probably infinite loop).
  FATAL ERROR: Host_Error: WatchdogHandler called - server exiting.

## What it should count instead

A crash that matters happens after the server has settled and while a wave is
being measured. Two things separate it from the noise:

- it is not preceded by the install line
- it carries a cause worth printing, and the two seen so far are
  WatchdogHandler and a plain segfault with neither

So: count crashes only after the "watching for N wave results" mark, and print
the WatchDog line when there is one, because "crashed 1 time(s)" and "the
watchdog killed it after an engineer was stuck for 12s" send you to completely
different places.
close_reason: Filed on a wrong inference. I thought the crash count included install-time restarts because each 'core dumped' was preceded by 'installed the bots and the statistics plugin'; that line prints every thirty seconds for the whole run, so it separates nothing. run.sh already scopes the count to this run's window and was right. What it could still do is print the cause, and that is worth having: 'crashed 1 time(s)' and 'the watchdog killed it after an engineer was stuck 12s' send you to different places. Refiled as that, narrowly.

title: A taunting bot holds the wave instead of readying
description:
Reported from a nightly run: a bot in a taunt animation does not press F4, and
the wave waits on it.

## Cause

`SetPlayerReady` announces readiness with a client command:

    FakeClientCommand(client, "tournament_player_readystate %d", state)

A taunt holds that. Because the command only goes out while the flag disagrees,
it is reissued every frame until it lands, so a short taunt merely delays the
ready and nobody notices.

A looping taunt does not end on its own. Then the command never lands, the flag
never flips, and the team sits at the ready screen waiting on a bot doing a
dance with no way to see which bot or why.

## Fix

`ReadyDefender` wraps the readiness calls in `UpdateDefenderReadiness` and ends
the taunt before saying ready:

    if (state && TF2_IsPlayerInCondition(actor, TFCond_Taunting))
        TF2_RemoveCondition(actor, TFCond_Taunting);

Only when readying, never when un-readying, so nothing cancels a taunt during a
wave. Between rounds a taunt is worth nothing to anybody, so it loses to the
ready rather than the other way round.

This is correct whether or not the engine was the thing refusing the command. If
the taunt was blocking it, this unblocks it. If something else was, a bot that
is not taunting is one fewer thing between the wave and starting.

## Not verified against a looping taunt

The reasoning above is from the code, not from a reproduction. Worth confirming
with a bot on a looping taunt that the wave now starts, since that is the case
that turns a delay into a hang. Bot taunts come from the loadout slots in
`util.sp` (`TF_LOADOUT_SLOT_TAUNT` and the two after it), so a config that gives
one is the way to set it up.
close_reason: Fixed. ReadyDefender ends TFCond_Taunting before setting ready, only on the readying path. Not reproduced against a looping taunt, which is the case that turns a delay into a hang; noted in the bead.

title: The teleporter exit is built inside the blast that kills the sentry
description:
Reported from a nightly run on Decoy: the engineers put their sentry beside
their teleporters, which reads as bad placement to anybody watching.

It is not a placement failure. It is the design, and the mod's own constants say
why it is wrong.

## The numbers already in the repo

`source/redbots3/behavior/engineerbuildteleporter.sp` anchors the exit to the
nest, and says plainly what the nest is:

    /* The exit stands off the nest centre rather than on it
       The nest centre is where the sentry is ... */
    #define TELEPORTER_EXIT_RADIUS  150.0

So the exit is always 150 units from the sentry, deliberately. Meanwhile
`source/redbots3/util.sp`:

    #define BUSTER_BLAST_RANGE  400.0

150 is well inside 400. The mod knows how far a sentry buster reaches, uses that
number to make bots run away, and then parks the teleporter exit at less than
half of it from the thing busters are sent to kill.

One buster takes the sentry and the exit together, every time. So does a giant
demo's spam or a tank's path. The engineer's whole investment sits in one blast
radius, and the team loses its forward spawn at exactly the moment the sentry
falls, which is when they most need to get back.

## Why the radius is that small

The comment explains the constraint it was solving, and it is a real one: eight
stand points aimed at the nest centre are eight looks at the sentry and eight
refused placements, so the spot walks around the nest and the engineer stands
between the two. 150 is "far enough out not to be inside his own sentry".

That is a build-validity radius, not a tactical one. It answers "where can he
physically place it" and never asks "where should it be".

## What to change

Separate the two questions. The exit needs its own spot chosen for survival and
usefulness, with the nest as a hint rather than an anchor:

- Outside `BUSTER_BLAST_RANGE` of the sentry. That single rule is most of the
  fix and the constant already exists.
- Still close enough to the fight that arriving players are useful, and still
  reachable, which is what the existing stand-point walk is good at.
- Not on the robots' path, or the exit is destroyed on the way past.

The map configs already support a hand-placed answer. Decoy declares
`TeleporterExit` at `-361 -159 573` while its nests are at `292 598 544`,
`214 537 364` and `-218 737 360`, so the configured exit is nowhere near a nest.
Check whether that configured spot is being used at all, because a run that
builds 150 units off the nest is not using it.

The Decoy config also declares no `TeleporterEntrance` at all: its
`Config_LoadMap` line reads `0 tele-in, 1 tele-out`. The entrance falls back to
stepping 200 units out of the spawn door toward the nest, which is why an
entrance can end up beside a nest that happens to sit near spawn. Whether the
entrance wants a configured spot per map is the smaller half of this.

## Test

The testbed already walks nests. Add a check that no teleporter is built within
`BUSTER_BLAST_RANGE` of a friendly sentry, and run it on Decoy and Coal Town.
That is the regression test and the acceptance test at once.
close_reason: Fixed in e20deb3. The exit now tries a ring at BUSTER_BLAST_RANGE + 100 all the way round before falling back to the old 150-unit ring, so a cramped map still gets an exit rather than none. Root cause was narrower than the bead said: Decoy names one TeleporterExit spot and NearestFreeExitSpot hands it to the first engineer, so with two engineers the second finds it taken, returns false, and drops to the nest-anchored fallback. That fallback was the unsafe path.

title: Bots look like they ready up but the ready does not register
description:
vixon2: "they sound like they're readying up but it doesn't go through"

Came out of Jebby asking how to stop the autofill bots auto-readying after each
wave, which EZKSupernova answered was already changed: "as of the latest
version, they only ready up when you do". vixon2's symptom is the opposite
failure and was not followed up. Unconfirmed.

title: Engineers do not replace a destroyed dispenser
description:
Cowser, in a list of bot suggestions: engineers should "always prioritize
replacing the Dispenser when it is broken".

Filed as a report, not a confirmed defect: he asked for it as behaviour rather
than saying he watched one fail to rebuild.
close_reason:
Measured rather than assumed, and it is mostly already what he asks for. Across every run in results/, 1441 stretches of an engineer alive inside a wave with no dispenser of his own: median 20 seconds, quartiles 10 to 25, which is the time it takes him to walk over and build one. So he does prioritise it.

The tail is real though: 58 stretches over a minute and a worst of 165 seconds. The cause is in the code rather than in the measurement - the dispenser branch in CTFBotMvMEngineerIdle_Update only fires when m_ctSentrySafe is in the future, so on a wave where the sentry is under fire continuously he never gets a window and the dispenser stays down for the rest of it. That is a defensible order, the sentry is the nest, and it is also exactly the wave where the team would want the dispenser.

Closing as measured. If it should change, the change is that gate and the number to hold it against is the tail above, not the median.

title: A refused purchase ended the whole shopping trip
description:
Forty five shopping trips measured on Bavarian Botbash: ten of them ended because
the game refused a purchase, and one of those walked away with 700 credits still
in the wallet. The reasoning in the code was that the ranking would pick the same
line again and be refused until the window ran out, which is true and is an
argument for remembering the refusal rather than for giving up on the trip.

`m_bRefusedUpgrade` is per trip. A refused line is skipped for the rest of it and
the next interval picks the next thing down. Upgrade steps a wave are unchanged
at a median of 17, which is what should happen: the trips that were ending early
now spend what they had left.

The exit reason is logged either way:

    [tf2_defenderbots.smx] Shopping: <name> stopped, <why>, <n> credits left
close_reason: Fixed in a87d742: the refusal is remembered for the trip and the next interval picks the next line down. Upgrade steps a wave unchanged at a median of 17.

title: The medic's patient
description:
`PreferredPatient` in `nextbot_behavior.sp` works out who the medigun should be
on: the most maximum health, which names the Heavy without a class table and
follows the health upgrades the team buys. `behavior/medicheal.sp` acts on it by
doing the healing itself rather than by arguing with the game's own action.

Writing the patient into the game's action is still off, and the reason is worth
keeping: `action.SetHandleEntity(ACTION_HEAL_PATIENT_OFFSET, ...)` segfaulted the
server on the first Mannhattan run, with no watchdog line, which is a memory
fault rather than a slow frame. The offset is a hardcoded field inside one of the
game's own actions. Everything else in this mod only reads it, and the difference
matters: reading a wrong offset gives a wrong answer, writing one corrupts
whatever is really there.

What was reported and is fixed: the medic stood in the house in the middle of
Coaltown for a whole wave. The candidate list was the team within nine metres, so
once the Heavy walked out of that the ask came back with the engineer at his nest
and could never come back with anybody else. The list is the whole team now, a
healthy engineer is not on it because his own dispenser is doing that job, and
the answer is held between asks because the gate that decides whether the medic
heals at all runs every frame and every ask is a path computation per teammate.

What is still open is where he should stand once he has a patient. He follows the
patient, and nothing in this mod says where the team holds, which is the same gap
item 3 records for nest scoring.
notes:
Imported from TODO.md item 14 — section: Behaviour and map data
Original heading: The medic's patient. Mostly closed

title: The Spy tells that are about behaviour
description:
What is implemented is a Spy who is close and appeared out of nowhere. What a
human actually reads is a teammate walking against the flow of the team, one
who never shoots at anything, and one whose class is not in a lineup the bots
themselves chose.

That last one is nearly free here, because the mod picks the RED team and knows
exactly which classes it asked for. A RED Heavy on a team with no Heavy in it is
a Spy, and no human on the server would have to be told.
notes:
Imported from TODO.md item 8 — section: Behaviour and map data
Original heading: The Spy tells that are about behaviour. Open

comments.author: m-this
comments.text: Watch out for mvm-3it when you build these tells. The tell proposed here — a RED class that is not in the lineup the bots chose — fires on the human player every time, because his class is never one the mod picked. SwagDoll420 already reports the bots calling him out as an enemy Spy. Adding this tell as written would make that worse, not better.

title: Nothing senses which way the robots came
description:
The nest scorer reasons about the bomb and about static mesh data. `BOMB_DROP`,
nav visibility, the spawn room flags and `bot_hint_sentrygun` are all baked at
map compile time and identical every wave. The only dynamic inputs are the
bomb's position, which resets to the same place each wave, and `BLOCKED`, which
is now read.

So on a map where the mesh does not change and only the spawn door differs,
`ShouldRelocateNest` computes a gain near zero and correctly does nothing.
Mannworks is exactly that map, and it is where the note asking for this was
written.

The cheap way in is to watch the robots instead of the map. Sample live BLU
players on a timer, map each to a nav area, count visits per area, and use
"where robots actually walked" as the approach sample in place of the radius
around the bomb, falling back to today's sample when the count is empty. It is
one wave behind by construction: wave N is chosen from wave N-1's traffic,
which is right whenever the spawn side repeats and wrong exactly once when it
flips.

Parsing the popfile would know the route before the wave instead of after. It
is a text parser for a format with no schema, plus a file location problem on
custom missions, for information that arrives one wave later for free.
notes:
Imported from TODO.md item 9 — section: Behaviour and map data
Original heading: Nothing senses which way the robots came. Open

title: The sticky launchers that want playing differently
description:
`behavior/stickytrap.sp` handles the stock launcher. A Quickiebomb wants its
shots charged, and a Scottish Resistance wants bombs kept in several places at
once and detonated selectively, which is a different behaviour rather than a
tuning of this one.

Either could be refused outright instead, so the loadout code hands the bot a
launcher the existing behaviour already plays well.
notes:
Imported from TODO.md item 6 — section: Behaviour and map data
Original heading: The sticky launchers that want playing differently. Open

title: Nothing deploys the Medic's Projectile Shield
description:
Every guide puts one tick of it first for a Medic and they are right about a
person: it is the strongest single thing a Medic does to a wave. It is deployed
with the special attack key, and no behaviour in this mod has ever pressed one.

So `generate rage on heal` was three hundred credits at the top of the Medic's
list buying a meter that fills a button nobody uses. It is refused in
`IsUpgradeWasted` until something presses it, and the moment something does it
goes straight back to the top.

The wider point is worth keeping: the wiki is written for people, and a
recommendation is only worth copying where this mod's bots can do the thing it
assumes. Three of them failed that test in one pass. The Pyro's Destroy
Projectiles is an airblast the Phlogistinator has not got. Jump height reaches
credits a person can see on a ledge, and a bot walks where the nav mesh says.
And this one.

The two that passed are worth naming too, because the test is not "distrust the
guide": the Sniper really does aim at the head bone, so Explosive Headshot earns
its place at the top, and the Engineer's own play-tested ordering beat the page.
notes:
Imported from TODO.md item 6b — section: Behaviour and map data
Original heading: Nothing deploys the Medic's Projectile Shield. Open
close_reason:
Implemented and measured. The button is pressed now: MedicProjectileShield puts the shield up when the rage meter is full and something is shooting near his patient, and generate rage on heal is no longer refused in IsUpgradeWasted when the feature is on. It fires 26 to 35 times a run, logged, so a null result cannot be mistaken for a behaviour that never ran.

Three arms against the 24 attempt baseline on Bavarian Botbash wave 1: held 176s/58 robots, 240s/83, and 175s/60, against a baseline of 160s and 58 with quartiles of 154-192 and 52-64. The middle arm is outside the band on both and did not replicate, and the first shared the machine with another server. Two of three sit inside the band.

So it ships off, behind medic_shield, and the item's own premise is settled: the wiki is right that a person should press it, and this mod can now press it. Whether it is worth three hundred credits is what the switch is for.

comments.author: m-this
comments.text: Reopened the decision, not the issue: shipping on. Three arms could not tell it apart from the baseline, and the reason to keep it anyway is one the bed cannot measure - every run here is bots alone, and a shield between a robot's rockets and a human player is worth something none of these numbers count. medic_shield defaults on now.

title: A nest is scored for the bomb and not for the team
description:
`ScoreNestArea` weighs range to the bomb, height, room and spacing from the
other engineers. It does not know where the rest of the lineup is standing.

A nest the team walks through is a dispenser that heals somebody and a sentry
with bodies in front of it. A nest nobody passes is an engineer alone. Distance
to where the team holds belongs in that score, and the reason it is not there
yet is that nothing in this mod says where the team holds.
notes:
Imported from TODO.md item 4 — section: Behaviour and map data
Original heading: A nest is scored for the bomb and not for the team. Open

comments.author: m-this
comments.text: Two reports that the nest position ignores pressure. k-kaneta: "he tries to make nest at set position no matter how hard you are pushed, which means he just waltz into robot swarm and just dies". Cowser's suggestion: engineers "can move spots based on the Bomb's location, and will reset to the base location between waves".

title: The Demoman is the weakest seat, and it is in every lineup
description:
A sweep of every map put it at 1634 damage a wave across forty waves, against
the Heavy's 8594, with a seat in all seven lineups.

It is not aim. 308 damage a kill is better than the Pyro's 354 and the Heavy's
425: it is efficient with what it fires and does not fire enough.

Holding the launcher by default was tried and measured and it is worse. Six
waves of Coaltown either way, one build, one switch between them:

| | damage a wave | kills | cleared |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| pipes first | 1821 | 27 | 5 of 6 |
| stickies first | 880 | 11 | 4 of 6 |

Half the damage, so the switch is gone rather than left off. The hole in the
argument was that the bot fires at where a robot is rather than where it is
going: a sticky thrown at a walking robot lands behind it and catches nobody,
and the clip and the reload are spent for nothing where a pipe at least does its
damage when it connects.

Which leaves the trap, and the trap is the thing the guides are actually
describing when they say a Demoman's damage is in his secondary. Bombs go on
ground the robots have not reached yet, and the bot waits. `behavior/stickytrap.sp`
lays one, and it only ever runs when no threat is visible at all, on a twenty
second cooldown, so during a wave it never runs. That gate is the next thing to
move, and it wants measuring the same way this was.

Two smaller things went in alongside and are unmeasured, because they were in
both arms: a Medic is always worth the switch to the launcher, and detonation is
counted across the whole cluster rather than answered by the first bomb that
qualifies.
notes:
Imported from TODO.md item 6a — section: Behaviour and map data
Original heading: The Demoman is the weakest seat, and it is in every lineup. Open

title: Map data
description:
`mvm_bigrock`, `mvm_coaltown`, `mvm_decoy`, `mvm_mannworks`, `mvm_mannhattan`
and `mvm_rottenburg` now carry `EngineerNest`, `DispenserSpot` and
`TeleporterExit` blocks. Somebody flew each map and stood on each spot, so they
outrank the nav mesh reasoning and the map's own hint entities.

The raw capture is in `testbed/results/`: `spots.log` is what the command
printed, `chat.log` is what was said while printing it, and
`spots-annotated.tsv` joins the two and carries the corrections. Spots that
were dumped and then rejected are marked rejected rather than deleted, so a
coordinate that looks odd can be traced back to what was said about it.

What is left is the other twenty-two config files, none of which have been
walked. `sm_dump_spot <block> [aim]` prints the line to paste. Stand on the
spot for accuracy; `aim` traces the crosshair to the world, which is how a map
gets marked from above without landing on every spot.
notes:
Imported from TODO.md item 3 — section: Behaviour and map data
Original heading: Map data. Six maps done, the rest open
close_reason: Closed

title: Teleporters
description:
They are built. What was wrong was three separate things and none of them was
the map data:

- The entrance spot was the spawn point plus the direction to the nest times a
  distance, which is a line drawn through whatever wall is in the way. It reads
  the nav mesh's route from the engineer to the spawn point now, and samples it
  backwards from the spawn end, so the attempts walk the way a player walks.
- The exit spot was the nest centre, which is where the sentry is, so all eight
  attempts asked the game to put a teleporter inside a sentry gun. It stands off
  the centre now and he stands between the two.
- On a team of nothing but bots the wave started the instant the last nest
  finished, so the build action gave up on its first update with "Wave started".
  `IsDefenderPrepared` holds the ready for the teleporter, but only when there
  is no human on the server: a player who has finished shopping should not be
  held for a building the bots want, and their shopping is already the time the
  engineer needs.

The order was the open question and the 1.9.0 play-test answered it. EZKSupernova:
"they should stop insta-teleporting to the front to build a sentry and dispenser
because now they run all the way back to spawn to place the entrance then go to
place the exit; the warp to the front only works if they place the exit first
then use the tele once they place the entrance."

So it is exit first. The engineer is already at the nest when the wave ends,
which is where the exit goes, and walking back to spawn for the entrance is the
walk the teleporter exists to remove. Building the exit first means the entrance
is the only trip, and after it he rides his own teleporter forward.

The argument for entrance first was that an exit alone moves nobody, and that is
true of a half-built pair, but it has the trip the wrong way round: the engineer
is the first passenger.

Measure it rather than assuming, because the reason for the old order was also
an argument. `testbed/` reports time spent walking and dispenser uptime, and a
mission either way on a map with a long approach, Rottenburg or Mannhattan, says
whether the engineer reaches his nest earlier. Add the telemetry first if the
report does not already carry time-to-first-sentry, because that is the number
this changes.

No official map names a `TeleporterEntrance` and none needs to: the route out of
spawn is read from the mesh. The six that name a `TeleporterExit` still use it.
notes:
Imported from TODO.md item 5 — section: Behaviour and map data
Original heading: Teleporters. Built now, exit first, and that wants measuring

comments.author: m-this
comments.text: EZKSupernova, on the build order: "I'm glad they build teleporters now, but they should stop insta-teleporting to the front to build a sentry and dispenser because now they run all the way back to spawn to place the entrance then go to place the exit" / "the warp to the front only works if they place the exit first then use the tele once they place the entrance". The bead says exit first; what he is seeing is the engineer warping forward before either end exists, which makes the entrance a walk back to spawn. Wants measuring against the current order.

title: The stuck watchdog carries a dead lurkingNowhere flag
description:
Found while porting UpdateStuckWatchdog to Go; carried across unchanged, because
a port does not fix.

The function computes:

  bool lurkingNowhere = false;
  bool wantsToBeElsewhere = g_arrPluginBot[actor].bPathing || myLoco.IsStuck()
      || noBehaviour || lurkingNowhere;

lurkingNowhere is assigned false and never assigned anything else, so the last
term of that disjunction is dead. Reading the history, it was the sniper's stall
before that moved into its own timer above (the shove problem: the watchdog's
timer is reset by teammates walking through a parked sniper, so the sniper's
stall had to be timed from the last moment he was doing his job). The variable
is what is left of the earlier shape.

Nothing is broken. It is one wasted read a think per bot and a line that makes
the disjunction look like it has four reasons when it has three.

## Done when

The variable and the term are gone from internal/body/stuckwatch, and the
generated file no longer has them.

title: Generated out-parameters are zeroed, the shipped ones are not
description:
A generated function zeroes its out-parameters at entry. The shipped SourcePawn does not: NearestConfiguredSpot only assigns spot when it finds something nearer, so a caller's buffer keeps its old value when the answer is false.

Seen on a live server after the teleporter port: sm_dump_nest printed 'teleporter target: mode 0 at 0 0 0' where the old code would have printed whatever the spot held before.

Behaviour is the same at both call sites today, because both check the bool before reading the vector. It is a difference in what an unwritten out-parameter holds, and it belongs in a bead rather than in a fix that rides along with a port.

title: About 190 lines that are watched and never acted on
description:
Found by the parity inventory. Each is dead weight that reads as behaviour.

events.sp 181-226, a behaviour reset ticker superseded by PATHS_PER_FRAME. ReportEngineerStall and the range repair counter, whose own comment says it is watched and not acted on. The SayClimb bisect instrumentation. markgiant's ForgetAllKnownEntities aim hack. redbots_debug_old_wedge_recovery with a 0.1 second timer that runs forever doing nothing. A dead lurkingNowhere OR term. Two contradictory comment blocks on ShouldTakeUpPosition. An unconditional LogMessage per shield deploy. blu_assist documentation describing two levers that do not exist.

The inventory refuted one candidate it expected to find: the 120 line dead stock block in util.sp has callers for all seven names.

title: EntIndexToHScript comes from a SourceMod newer than the vendored includes
description:
The one genuinely unaccounted call site out of 1216. The plugin calls it, the include tree does not declare it.

So the vendored SourceMod is older than the one the plugin is built against, which is worth knowing on its own: build.sh pins a tarball and something has drifted past it.

Either move the pin forward or record why it stays. A binding generator that reads includes older than the compiler is generating against the wrong API.
notes:
Not drift. There is nothing to move the pin for.

The plugin's one EntIndexToHScript is inside a string: util.sp:3205 passes it to OSLib_RunScriptCode, so it is Squirrel executed by the game's VScript VM, not a SourcePawn native. bindings.Code already blanks string literals, and with it the count is zero unbound natives and zero unbound members over 1085 free call sites and 188 member uses. The vendored SourceMod is not older than the compiler and build.sh's pin stays.

The reason it read as unaccounted for so long is worse than the finding. TestUnbound was skipping. internal/bindgen, internal/bindings and internal/navmesh each resolved MVMBOTS_UPSTREAM themselves and each got it wrong: a relative path was read from the package directory rather than the repository root, so bindgen and navmesh reported ok in under a second while running none of their proofs.

All three now go through internal/upstream. upstream.SkipOrFail skips with the variable named when the repository is absent and fails when MVMBOTS_REQUIRE_UPSTREAM is set, which make check sets, the same shape as MVMBOTS_REQUIRE_SPSHELL. Under the gate those two packages now take 78 and 66 seconds under -race, which is the size of what was not running.

The bindings goldens for actions and actions_processors were stale for the same reason and are regenerated.
close_reason: Closed

title: Fuzz the float literal round trip through spcomp
description:
The spike's literal() uses shortest round trip decimal in 'f' form and has not been tested against denormals or very large magnitudes, where spcomp's lexer may not read back the same float32.

A generated constant that does not survive the compiler is a silent wrong answer in every generated function that holds one.

Fuzz literal, then spcomp, then spshell, comparing bits. Cheap, and it pins the thing the whole differential test rests on.
notes:
Done, and it found the bug it was filed to look for. FuzzFloatLiteralSurvivesTheCompiler writes a float32 as a literal, compiles it, echoes it back through spshell and compares bits. The plugin computes nothing, so a difference is the compiler reading what Go wrote and nothing else.

The seed corpus failed immediately on FLT_MAX: literal wrote it as 39 digits in 'f' form and spcomp compiled 0x5f794ad1, about 1.8e19, with no diagnostic. Exactly the silent wrong answer the bead predicted.

The comment on literal was also wrong. spcomp does take exponent form, under two rules that are easy to get wrong and both silent-ish: the mantissa needs a point with a digit each side, so 1e-45 is 'number literal has invalid digits' and 1.0e-45 is the smallest denormal; and a positive exponent carries no sign, so 3.4028235e+38 is 'exponential must be followed by integer'. literal now formats with 'g', adds the point and strips the plus.

151368 executions over five minutes with no failure, on top of the seeded denormal floor, normal floor and ceiling, the ends of exact integer range and negative zero.

literal is the only float formatter in the repository today: nothing in spgen, tables or bindings writes a float literal, so this is the whole surface.
close_reason: Closed

title: Hand edits to generated SourcePawn cannot be committed
description:
This repository has no Makefile, only testbed/build.sh. It gets one, and make check is the gate.

From starter-kits: generated code is gitignored and the build verifies that generation succeeds and the output compiles, and CI runs Make targets rather than raw commands so the gate runs the same locally. A hand edit to generated SourcePawn then cannot be committed, because the generated files are not in the tree to edit.

Also the git hooks: .git/hooks held only samples until 2026-08-29, so bd never ran on a commit here and omae-beads saw nothing. bd hooks install fixes it, and a fresh clone needs it run again. The Makefile should have a target that does it.
notes:
Done. The go repository has a Makefile with make check as the gate: go vet, the linter, go test -race, generation run twice with the outputs diffed, and go build over the generated tree. gen/ is gitignored, so there is no generated SourcePawn in the tree to hand edit, which is the property the bead asked for rather than a rule somebody has to remember.

The hooks half is done in ../tf2-mvm-bots, which is where the database is: core.hooksPath points at .beads/hooks and all five shims are installed. The go repository deliberately gets none. It has no beads database, so a bd hook on a commit here would look for one on every commit and find nothing. A make target that installed them would be a target that installs a broken hook.
close_reason: Closed

title: The rest of the pure decisions move a class at a time
description:
After threat priority proves the loop: upgrade order, nest spot scoring, medic patient choice, sniper perch choice, sticky placement scoring. Each is arithmetic with no engine in it.

One class per pass, each with its own golden inputs, each measured on the test-bed before the previous one is called done. Not a sweep.

Split into its own beads when the first one starts. This is a placeholder so the list does not read as if the epic ends at threat priority.
notes:
Cheapest first body identified by the subset survey over 4511 lines of behavior/: the ten EvalTankWeapon_* functions at attacktank.sp:294-600 are already inside the subset apart from int becoming int32. Start there rather than with an engineer action.

The survey's headline: across those 4511 lines there is nothing that is both pure decision logic and lacks an in-subset spelling. The subset does not need widening to reach parity on decisions.

title: Frames still hitch to about 140 ms on Mannhattan
description:
What is left of mvm-cf3 after the wedge recovery, at its own size.

Mannhattan, six waves, with the fix in: worst frame about 140 ms, three to six
frames over the 100 ms mark per six waves, and 60 to 85 frames over 30 ms.

That is a hitch rather than the server stopping. The reported symptom was a
two second freeze and that is gone: 1833 ms became 141 ms. But a player did
report noticing a stutter at 113 ms, so this is above what somebody can feel.

Not a P0 and not urgent. Worth knowing the shape before spending on it:

- Decoy never passes 100 ms and Mannhattan does, so it is the map or its mesh
  rather than the mod's per-frame work in general
- FEATURE_PATH_LENGTH_CAP exists and is off. It moved stalls from 6 to 3 and the
  worst median from 130 to 104 across six waves, which does not clear the
  spread. Turning it on is one line if a better measurement ever wants it
- 28 of 29 path computes now go through the two helpers, so bounding them all is
  a change in one place rather than twenty

title: The test-bed says a crash happened but not what kind
description:
run.sh ends a crashed run with "the game server has crashed N time(s)" and a
grep to run by hand. The count is correct. What it does not say is which of two
very different things happened, and they lead opposite ways:

- the engine watchdog killing a long frame, which shows as
  "WatchDog! Server took too long to process" and means something is slow
- a plain SIGSEGV, which means something is corrupt

Tonight both happened in one evening and looked identical from the summary.

Print the WatchDog line when there is one, and name the core file when there is
one, since testbed/symbolise-core.sh turns it into a stack in a single command
and finding it was the slow part.
close_reason: Done. run.sh now says which kind of crash it was and prints the two commands that turn the newest core into a stack. Verified against tonight's logs.

title: Confirm the disposable sentry result on a second map
description:
mvm-8ws turned `sm_redbots_feature_engineer_disposable` off on one map's
evidence. The evidence was strong — six waves of Decoy per arm with
non-overlapping death spreads, [0,3,5,7,9,10] against [11,12,14,15,15,17] — but
it is still one map.

Run `testbed/ab.sh --feature engineer_disposable --maps "mvm_coaltown
mvm_mannworks"` and check the same three numbers: defender deaths per wave,
sentries lost, waves cleared.

Two things to watch for, because either would change the answer rather than
confirm it:

- A map with more nest spots may pay for the second gun where Decoy's three do
  not. If Coaltown comes out the other way, the priority wants to read the nest
  count rather than being one number for every map.
- The two Decoy arms ran under different machine load. Durations are not
  comparable across that and were not used; deaths, sentries and clears should
  not care, and a rerun with both arms under the same load would say so for
  certain.

If the second map agrees, this is settled and the switch can eventually go: a
feature nobody turns on is a branch to delete. If it disagrees, the switch has
earned its place and the default becomes a per-map question.

title: Cosmetics throw on bots, and the hat is silently lost
description:
Not reported by anybody. Found in Cowser's debug bundle while triaging the
seven-player report, in `sourcemod/errors_20260824.log`.

    [SM] Exception reported: Assertion failed - wearable entity 589 not attached
         to player. Gamedata may need to be updated
    [SM] Blaming: tf2utils.smx
    [SM]   [3] TF2Util_EquipPlayerWearable
    [SM]   [4] Line 221, .../redbots3/cosmetics.sp::WearHat
    [SM]   [5] Line 129, .../redbots3/cosmetics.sp::Timer_GiveBotCosmetics

Three times across two maps (rottenburg and coaltown), each on a different
wearable entity, so it is not one bad item id.

Low priority on its own: the throw is caught by SourceMod, the bot plays fine,
and only the hat is lost. It is filed because an unhandled exception in a timer
is the kind of thing that stops being cosmetic later, and because the log line
suggests the real cause is elsewhere.

## Worth checking

The tf2utils assertion says the wearable is not attached to the player at the
moment we equip it. Two readings, and they want different fixes:

- We are equipping too early, before the bot's wearable is attached. Then the
  fix is ours: check attachment before calling, or move the work later in
  `Timer_GiveBotCosmetics`.
- tf2utils' own gamedata is stale, which is what the message literally suggests.
  Then the fix is a version bump, and we should confirm the pinned tf2utils is
  current before writing any code.

Check the second one first, since it is a version lookup rather than a debug
session.

Separately, `WearHat` should handle the failure rather than let it throw. The
same log shows the hat pool already dropping items it knows a class cannot wear
("Item 30928 cannot be worn by class 1 and has been dropped from the hat pool"),
so the surrounding code already has a way to say no. This path should use it.
notes: The throwing equip now lives in the generated cosmetics.sp (internal/body/cosmetics.WearHat), not in source/redbots3/cosmetics.sp. The port carried the behaviour across unchanged, including clearing g_iEquipping on the way in: the fix, when it comes, goes in the Go.

title: Native Linux servers crash far more than Docker or Windows
description:
Reported from play: a native Linux server crashes far more often than the same
mod under Docker or on Windows. Not measured here, and the test-bed is Linux
inside Docker, so this is the one platform nothing in this repo exercises.

What is known, in order of how much evidence there is.

**A file replaced under a running server is fatal on Linux and refused on
Windows.** This repo has already been bitten by it once: `testbed/entrypoint.sh`
copied the staged tree over the running server every thirty seconds with `cp -r`,
and `cp` truncates before it writes. A loaded extension is mmap'd, truncating the
file invalidates the pages under it, and the next instruction out of that
extension is a SIGBUS. Five or six crashes in ten minutes, with the backtrace
naming whichever extension the loop had just rewritten. Windows refuses to
overwrite a file a running process has mapped, so the same deploy silently does
nothing instead of corrupting the server, and a Wine run that happened to have no
supervising loop read as a platform difference for a day. `cp -ru`, or stop the
server before copying.

**So the first question is whether the native deploy writes into a live server
directory** while it runs: an update script, a sync, an editor saving into
`tf/addons`. That is the shape that produces "Linux crashes more" with no code
difference at all.

**Memory pressure.** The watchdog measures frame time, and a page fault that
stalls a frame is indistinguishable from an infinite loop. A session went from
six clean waves to four failed runs in a row with 200 MB free and swap-in at
20 MB/s, code unchanged. `run.sh` refuses to start below 1500 MB now for exactly
this reason.

**Docker hides crashes.** The container restarts srcds by itself, so a crash
there reads as a hiccup while the same crash natively ends the session. Some of
the difference may be reporting rather than rate.

To settle it rather than guess, get a symbolised backtrace. Enable core dumps,
then copy `bin/`, `tf/bin/` and `tf/addons/sourcemod/{bin,extensions}` out of the
server and point gdb at them:

    gdb -batch -ex 'set sysroot /tmp/tfdbg' \
        -ex 'set solib-search-path /tmp/tfdbg/bin:/tmp/tfdbg/tf/bin:...' \
        -ex 'bt 25' /tmp/tfdbg/srcds_linux core.NNN

An unsymbolised trace is what kept the last one open for two sessions; with the
libraries in place it named the frame in one go.
notes:
Deprioritised, P1 to P3, and worked around rather than solved.

The launcher now passes -nowatchdog on Linux and only on Linux
(srcdsArgs in launcher/internal/runtime/runtime.go, where -nocrashdialog
already splits the two platforms; test TestTheWatchdogIsOffOnLinuxOnly).

The evidence is from the stress session that took the desktop down with it. The
watchdog build died inside nine minutes at load 7-8. The same load against
-nowatchdog held rcon on all twelve probes with no restart. That matches the
shape of the report: Docker and Windows are not affected, and the watchdog is
what kills a Linux server on a slow frame that neither of the others treats as
fatal.

What is given up is the kill on a genuinely hung frame, so a real infinite loop
now hangs where it used to restart. That is the better failure. It leaves a live
process to attach to instead of a core, and every hang this mod has actually
produced was a slow frame rather than a hang: mvm-297 was an unbounded nav mesh
search that tripped the watchdog and was fixed with PATHS_PER_FRAME.

Left at P3 rather than closed because the underlying question is untouched: why
a native Linux server takes frames long enough to trip a watchdog that Docker on
the same kernel does not. Nothing here answers that. If the crash reports stop,
this can close as won; if they keep coming with no watchdog in the picture, the
cause was never the watchdog and this bead is where that gets picked up.

Docker is deliberately not changed. It is not the platform being reported, its
arguments come from the upstream image's entry.sh rather than from us, and
changing an unaffected platform would remove the comparison this bead rests on.

testbed/run-native.sh takes TESTBED_SRCDS_EXTRA so a run can be pointed either
way without editing the script, which is how the two builds were compared.

comments.author: m-this
comments.text:
There is a native bed now, mvm 7beba7e:

    testbed/seed-native.sh                 once, copies the game out of the container
    testbed/run-native.sh --waves 12       same flags as run.sh
    testbed/symbolise-core.sh core.1234    a backtrace with names in it

It runs srcds_linux directly rather than through srcds_run, so a crash stays
crashed and leaves a core instead of being restarted underneath the measurement,
which is the thing the container bed cannot show. It writes the same server.cfg
as the container by sourcing entrypoint.sh, so the two beds differ in the one
variable this is about.

Three things it cost, all worth knowing for anyone standing one up:

- The exclude when copying the game has to be anchored. An unanchored core.*
  also matches SourceMod's core.games.txt and core.phrases.txt; the server then
  starts, fails to parse its gamedata and never answers rcon.
- srcds takes the console over after the Steam banner and writes nothing more to
  a redirected stdout. That reads exactly like a server that never started.
  Readiness is asked of rcon.
- The host needs a 32 bit C++ runtime. Rather than a package, seed-native.sh puts
  the image's own into the game's bin/, which srcds_run already has on its
  library path.

Running a native sample now. Whatever it says, the recipe is the useful half:
the same three commands on the machine that actually crashes will produce a
symbolised backtrace, and that is what this issue is short of.

comments.author: m-this
comments.text:
Measured with the whole player stack, and it does not reproduce here.

The native bed now loads tf2-archipelago's plugin beside the bots
(TESTBED_ARCHIPELAGO_SMX) and the bridge runs in test mode, so the integration is
genuinely live: the fake room recorded checks and death-link traffic while the
run played. Native srcds, the bots mod, the archipelago plugin and a bridge, on
Debian 13, alone on the machine:

                          waves  worst frame in a wave  slow  stalled  worst before a wave
  native, bots only         12          87 ms            274     0          146 ms
  native + archipelago       7          82 ms            245     0          109 ms

No crash, no stalled frame, and the wave start is if anything quieter with the
plugin than without. So on this machine the integration does not trip the
watchdog, and the plugin's own mvm_begin_wave handler is three integer
assignments and one timer, with its debug logging compiled to an early return
when the convar is off.

What is still different from a player's server, in the order I would test them:

- The launcher runs srcds through srcds_run, this bed runs srcds_linux directly.
  srcds_run adds the restart loop and the steamclient dlopen.
- Humans connected. Every measurement here has an idle fake client and no real
  ones, and joining, choosing a class and the bot kicked to make room for them
  are all wave-start work this never does.
- Their hardware and what else it is doing. A page fault that stalls a frame is
  an infinite loop as far as the watchdog is concerned.

The decisive run is on the machine that crashes:

    TESTBED_NATIVE_ROOT=~/path/to/tf2ap/tf-dedicated testbed/run-native.sh --waves 12

and if it dies, testbed/symbolise-core.sh on the core it leaves. That gives a
named frame instead of 'it crashed', which is what this issue is short of.
